blocks.text: A saloon in the house of Violetta; in the back scene is a door, which opens into another saloon; there are also two side doors; on the left is a fireplace over which is a mirror.—In the center of the apartment is a dining-table very elegantly laid.
Violetta, seated on a couch, is conversing with the Doctor and some friends, whilst others are receiving the guests who arrive, among whom are the Baron, and Flora on the arm of the Marquis.

lines: The appointed time you have exceeded,
You are full late.
We lingered at Flora’s,
And, while playing, the hours seemed to fly.
Flora, and dear friends, the rest of the night
We’ll pass in joys more brilliant than the fête—
When the wine’s flowing, pleasure reigns always.
Can you thus find enjoyment?
Yes, truly;
In the dance and the song I find
The medicine which cures all my complaints.
Yes, enjoyment lengthens life.

blocks.text: Gastone, Alfred and Germont come forward, while servants are busy about the table.

lines: In Alfred Germont, O dear madam!
Behold another admirer, than whom
Few can boast a more sincere friend.
My dear Viscount, many thanks for the introduction.

blocks.text: She extends her hand to Alfred, who kisses it.

lines: Dearest Alfred!
Dear Marquis!
I told you
You would find pleasure mixed with friendship.

blocks.text: The servants have prepared the table during this dialogue.

lines: Is all ready?

blocks.text: To a servant, who bows assent.

lines: My dear friends, be seated;
At the banquet each heart will o’erflow.
That was well said—for from
The goblet’s brim all secret troubles fly.

blocks.text: They seat themselves, Violetta between Alfred and Gastone, and opposite to them Flora, the Marquis and the Baron; the rest take their seats promiscuously; there is a momentary silence, during which the dishes are passed round, and Violetta and Gastone converse in an undertone.

lines: Of you Alfred’s always thinking.
Are you joking?
You were ill, and each day he flew here
To learn if you were better.
Pray cease, sir,
I can be naught to him.
I speak truly.
Can it be so?—and why?—I know not.
Yes, all is true.
Well, then, I am grateful.
You, dear baron, were not thus enamored.
But I’ve only known you a twelvemonth
And he some minutes only.
’Twould have been quite as well had you not spoken.
I do not greatly like him.
Why not?
On the contrary I like him much.
And you, sir, are perfectly silent.
He requires your encouragement, madam.
I will be his Hebe.
And may you,
Like her, be immortal.
Thus drink we.
But, Baron, can you think of neither verse
Nor toast in this mirthful moment?
Then ’tis thou.
Yes, yes, a song, a song.
I am not a poet.
Art thou not a singer?
Will it please you?
Yes.
Yes?—Willingly.
Pay attention, all.
Yes, list to the song.
We’ll drink to the beauty that’s beaming around,
Where Nature’s own flowers are blooming;
Where none but the voices of happiness sound,
And our pathway the lovelight’s illuming.
We’ll drink to the god that is true to the heart,
For love from his vot’ries will never depart;
So we’ll drink while there’s love in the cup which we quaff,
Since ’tis love o’er the world reigns supreme.
We’ll drink to friendship firm and true.
While love the cup shall crown.
Come, bask in the pleasure that falls to our share,
For time to take wing’s ever prone,
And the flowers of love are exotics so rare,
Their odor’s scarce shed ere ’tis flown.
Be gay, for youth will soon depart,
And even love decay,
As brightest scenes will fade,
And memories pass away.
Be gay while youth undimmed by care
Invites to joy and love.
Ah! let us join in the toast,
In the song and the revelling,
Passing the night in mirthful pleasure,
While love shall teach us how to treasure
This paradise on earth.
Life is in enjoyment.
To one who knows not what love is.
Well, know then, I despise it.
Fate frowns upon me.
Ah! let us join in the toast,
In the song and the revelling,
Passing the night in mirthful pleasure,
While love shall teach us how to treasure
This paradise on earth.
What’s that?
Will you my friends like to join in dancing?
Oh! a happy thought—all are delighted—let us all at once go.
Alas!

blocks.text: Violetta takes a few steps, but is obliged to stop.

lines: What ails you?
Nothing, nothing.
What makes you pause, then?
Well go, now—O Heaven!

blocks.text: She is again obliged to pause.

lines: Again!
You are suffering!
O Heaven! what means it?
A trembling merely seized me—pray do not linger.

blocks.text: Motioning them to go into the other saloon.

lines: Shortly I will follow you.
Well, if you wish it.

blocks.text: All pass into the other saloon, except Alfred and Violetta.

lines: How deadly pale!
You here!
Has your indisposition ceased?
I’m better.
Ah! in this way you’ll kill yourself.
You must take more care, or your health will fail you.
But how can I?
Oh! wert thou mine, I’d keep the—watch
And guard thee well, ’gainst all the ills in life
What say’st thou?
Ah! can it be that some one regards me?
Well, in the world perhaps none may.
Not one?
None but myself, love.
Say’st thou truly?
Thy great love I had forgotten.
You’re laughing!—Oh! have you a heart?
A heart? Yes, truly—but why? wherefore that question?
Ah! if you had one you could not trifle thus.
Are you in earnest?
I’d not deceive you.
Is’t long since you first loved me?
Ah! yes, a whole year.
O happy day! to memory dear,
When first thy smile shone o’er me,
Thy beauty beamed before me,
And bade my heart to love.
Wildly then my bosom bounded,
Love’s mysterious chain surrounded,
Link by link my sense confounded,
While pain and pleasure filled my heart.
Oh! if ’tis true, then from me fly—
Friendship is all I offer;
I can not love, nor will I e’er
My fickle fortunes proffer;
I would not act a traitor’s part,
Seek out some heart more loving,
And having found the treasure,
Expel me from thy thoughts.
What are you doing?
We’re talking nonsense.
Ah, ah!—’tis well—continue!
Of love we’ll talk no more—do you agree?
I will obey you—I’ll go.
Oh! what a hurry!
First take this little flower.
And why?
That you may return it.
Oh! when?
When all its bloom has faded.
O Heaven! to-morrow?
Well, yes, to-morrow.
Ah! now, indeed, I’m happy!

blocks.text: Taking the flower in a transport.

lines: You still say you love me?
I dearly love thee!
Are you going?
I am.
Fare thee well.
I am quite happy.

blocks.text: Violetta and all the others, who return from the dancing-saloon.

lines: See, she comes, the chaste Aurora,
And forewarns us to be going.
Many thanks, O gentle lady!
For the pleasure we’ve enjoyed.
Now the town of fêtes is brimful;
’Tis the time then to be gay;
But repose at night is needful,
That we may enjoy the day.
’Tis wondrous!—most wondrous!
Those words upon my heart seem graven!
Yet, may this love not be a great misfortune?
What say’st thou, O my troubled soul?
No man in thee e’er waked love’s passion.
O joy! before to me a stranger, to love
And be beloved!—And can I spurn it, and
Prefer the heartless life in which I now indulge?
Ah! was it he who filled my heart
With wild tumultuous feeling,
When fancy, with her rainbow hues,
My every sense was stealing—
Was it this modest gentle youth,
That ever, in my dreaming,
Called on my fevered senses to wake my heart to love?
Wildly then my bosom bounded,
Love’s mysterious chain surrounding,
Link by link my sense confounding,
While pain and pleasure filled my heart.
Whilst yet a child, bright visions came,
And shed their magic influence o’er me,
The image of my future love
In mystic radiance stood before me.
My thoughts, where’er I wandered,
Still on his beauty pondered,
Whilst field and flower, conspiring,
The sweet illusion fled.

blocks.text: She stands for a moment in thought, then exclaims:

lines: A folly!—a folly!—a vain delusion!
Wretched woman!—lonely!
By all deserted in this populous desert
Which the world at large calls Paris,
What can I hope, or what accomplish?
From joy to joy still flying,
Then in the vortex end.

blocks.text: Air. Let me bask in every pleasure.

lines: Let me bask in every pleasure,
Folly ever without measure;
Let every day in which I live,
Be spent in rounds of joy.
Evermore may each day find me
Whirling on through pleasure’s round—
Leaving always care behind me,
Ever thus may I be found.
